questions.question: A statistician creates five complete versions of a dataset, each filled with different plausible values for the missing incomes, then pools the five model results. What imputation framework is she using?
questions.explanation: Multiple imputation generates several complete datasets with plausible fill-ins, fits the model on each, and pools results to capture missing-data uncertainty.

questions.question: Two patients sit equally far from the cohort mean in Euclidean terms, but one lies far off the data's correlated direction. Which distance measure, scaled by the covariance matrix, flags this multivariate outlier?
questions.explanation: Mahalanobis distance scales deviations by the inverse covariance, so a point off the correlated direction scores far despite a modest Euclidean distance.

questions.question: A 'zip_code' feature has 40,000 categories, making one-hot encoding infeasible; instead each category is replaced by the mean target value observed for that category. What encoding is this?
questions.explanation: Target (mean) encoding maps each category to a target statistic, keeping a single column for high-cardinality features but requiring care against leakage.

questions.question: On strictly positive measurements, residual spread grows with the fitted values, so the analyst fits a single power parameter lambda to stabilize variance and normalize errors. Which transformation is she applying?
questions.explanation: Box-Cox chooses a power lambda for positive data that best stabilizes variance and normalizes; for non-positive inputs Yeo-Johnson is needed instead.

questions.question: Before any model is trained, an analyst scores each feature against the target with a chi-squared test and keeps the top twenty. Which feature-selection approach is this?
questions.explanation: Filter methods rank features by standalone statistical tests (chi-square, correlation) independent of any model, unlike wrapper or embedded methods.

questions.question: On an imbalanced dataset, an analyst first interpolates new minority samples between neighbors, then removes Tomek-link borderline pairs to clean class overlap. Which combined resampling method is this?
questions.explanation: SMOTETomek chains SMOTE oversampling with Tomek-link removal, both enlarging the minority class and cleaning the decision boundary.

questions.question: An SVM is refit repeatedly, each round discarding the features with the smallest weights, until only ten features remain. Which wrapper feature-selection method is this?
questions.explanation: RFE trains the model, ranks features by importance (e.g., SVM weights), drops the weakest, and repeats until the target number remains.

questions.question: T-shirt sizes S, M, L, XL must be converted to numbers that preserve their natural ordering (S < M < L < XL). Which encoding is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Ordinal encoding assigns ordered integers to categories with a meaningful rank; one-hot would discard the ordering information.

questions.question: A sensor stream has multi-hour gaps; the analyst carries each last observed reading forward across the missing timestamps, respecting time order. Which imputation is this?
questions.explanation: Forward fill propagates the last valid observation across later gaps, a standard approach for temporal missing data.

questions.question: A stream classifier's error rate rises as the input distribution shifts; the monitoring method widens its window in stable periods and shrinks it when change is detected. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Adaptive windowing (e.g., ADWIN) adjusts the window size to the detected rate of change, reacting to concept drift in streams.

questions.question: A revenue-change feature contains zeros and negatives, so Box-Cox cannot be applied; which related power transformation handles non-positive inputs?
questions.explanation: Yeo-Johnson generalizes Box-Cox with a piecewise definition that accepts zero and negative values.

questions.question: Millions of distinct device IDs must become a fixed 1024-column matrix; each ID is passed through a hash function to pick its column. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Feature hashing (the hashing trick) maps arbitrary categories into a fixed number of columns via a hash function, trading collisions for bounded dimensionality.

questions.question: Fitting a Lasso model drives several coefficients to exactly zero during training, performing feature selection as a by-product of fitting. Which family of feature-selection methods is this?
questions.explanation: Embedded methods select features during model training itself — L1 penalties like Lasso's are the canonical example — unlike filter or wrapper methods.

questions.question: Sicker patients are less likely to complete a health survey, so nonresponse depends on the unobserved health status itself. Which missing-data mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: MNAR means missingness depends on the missing values themselves; if it depended only on observed columns it would be MAR.

questions.question: An analyst imputes each incomplete column by regressing it on all the other columns, iterating round-robin until the estimates stabilize, using scikit-learn. Which estimator is this?
questions.explanation: IterativeImputer models each feature with missing values as a function of the remaining features and iterates, inspired by chained-equations imputation.

questions.question: A feature ranges from a minimum of 40 to a maximum of 80. Using min-max normalization, what is the scaled value of an observation equal to 60?
questions.explanation: Min-max scaling computes (x - min) / (max - min) = (60 - 40) / (80 - 40) = 20 / 40 = 0.5.

questions.question: A column has mean 15 and standard deviation 5. What is the z-score (standardized value) of an observation equal to 25?
questions.explanation: z = (x - mean) / std = (25 - 15) / 5 = 2, meaning the value is two standard deviations above the mean.

questions.question: In a survey, income values are missing more often for younger respondents — the missingness relates to the observed 'age' column but not to the unobserved income itself. Which missing-data mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: MAR means missingness depends on observed variables, not on the missing values themselves; that would be MNAR.

questions.question: A categorical column has 12 unique categories. After one-hot encoding with one dummy dropped to avoid the dummy-variable trap, how many indicator columns are created?
questions.explanation: With k categories, dropping one reference level leaves k - 1 = 12 - 1 = 11 indicator columns.

questions.question: An analyst discretizes 'age' into 4 bins so that each bin contains approximately 25% of the observations. What type of binning is this?
questions.explanation: Quantile binning sets bin edges at quantiles so each interval holds roughly the same number of observations.
